title: Levon Helm - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 120,677 (the rest is navigation). Mark Lavon Helm, born 26 May 1940, Elaine, Arkansas; grew up in Turkey Scratch near Marvell; died 19 April 2012, New York City, of throat cancer. Saw Bill Monroe at six; guitar at eight, then drums; Grand Ole Opry on WSM, R&B on WLAC, Delta blues; his autobiography describes watching Sonny Boy Williamson's drummer James 'Peck' Curtis and imitating his R&B drumming. The Jungle Bush Beaters in high school; the Hawks full time after graduating in 1958; Toronto, Roulette 1959; 'Lavon' became 'Levon'. Left Dylan's tour in autumn 1965, replaced by touring drummers, 'most notably Mickey Jones'; back in autumn 1967. The Band's only American; the Last Waltz, 25 November 1976. RCO All-Stars (1977); Coal Miner's Daughter (1980), The Right Stuff (1983). Ringo Starr's All-Starr Band, 1989, drums, harmonica, singing The Weight and Up on Cripple Creek. This Wheel's on Fire (1993). Throat cancer late 1990s; 27 radiation treatments. Midnight Rambles; Dirt Farmer (2007, Grammy), Electric Dirt (2009, first Best Americana Album Grammy), Ramble at the Ryman (2011, Grammy). Around the Ramble period he switched to matched grip and a 'less busy, greatly simplified drumming style', away from the traditional grip of the Band years. Rolling Stone: No. 91 of the 100 Greatest Singers (2008), No. 22 of the 100 Greatest Drummers (2016). Springsteen on his drumming: 'You can't replicate it.'

title: The Band - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 178,948. Helm joined Hawkins in 1957, full time after high school in 1958; Danko (May 1961), Manuel (September 1961), Hudson last; split from Hawkins late 1963; the Levon Helm Sextet, Levon and the Hawks, the Canadian Squires (1965). Dylan's 1965 US tour and 1966 world tour: Helm left after a little more than a month; Bobby Gregg drums on 'One of Us Must Know'; Mickey Jones replaced Sandy Konikoff for the 1966 European leg. Helm back by October 1967. Albums: Big Pink (1968, John Simon), The Band (1969), Stage Fright (1970), Cahoots (1971), Rock of Ages (1972, Toussaint horns), Moondog Matinee (1973), Planet Waves and Before the Flood with Dylan (1974), Northern Lights - Southern Cross (1975), Islands (1977), The Last Waltz (1978); Jericho (1993), High on the Hog (1996), Jubilation (1998). Jon Carroll: Helm 'the only drummer who can make you cry'; 'Session drummer Jim Keltner admits to borrowing several of Helm's techniques.' Manuel credited with drums in the classic line-up.

title: Bryan Rogers, 'Levon Helm (1940-2012)', Encyclopedia of Arkansas
notes: Bill Monroe at six, guitar at eight; 'inspired shortly afterward to become a drummer' by F. S. Walcott's Rabbit's Foot Minstrels, which had a left-handed drummer; also by James 'Peck' Curtis, Sonny Boy Williamson's drummer; time at KFFA in Helena; guitar at twelve with his sister Linda on washtub bass; the Jungle Bush Beaters; met Ronnie Hawkins at seventeen at the West Helena Delta Supper Club, Hawkins without a drummer; top billing in Levon and the Hawks partly because he was in the musicians' union. Paul Evans (Rolling Stone Album Guide): 'the understated drive of Levon Helm's drumming'. Throat cancer; the Barn Burners; 'In 2005, Levon began singing again'; monthly Midnight Rambles at his Woodstock home; Ain't in It for My Health (2013).

title: Bob Girouard, 'Levon Helm: The Classic Drummer Interview', Classic Drummer, 2008 (with engineer Justin Guip)
notes: Six-page PDF, text extracted and read whole. After the 2008 Grammys for Dirt Farmer. Helm: 'Most of the things I play certainly have a street-beat-march to them. So, it's between that and watching Peck Curtis play with Sonny Boy Williamson and The King Biscuit Boys. That march and that shuffle is where I live most of the time.' On playing behind the beat: 'It's about the rhythm section. Look at Muscle Shoals... Roger Hawkins and David Hood or Al Jackson and Duck Dunn from Memphis.' Grip: 'in the old days I used traditional grip about 80% of the time. I developed a habit of being overly busy with my left hand... When I got sick and was playing blues with the Barn Burners (with Little Sammy Davis), the backbeat became much more important. By changing my grip to mallet-style it basically simplified everything.' Set-up (interviewer): snare, two toms and kick, a 20-inch (earlier 18-inch) ride with rivets, a 16- or 17-inch crash with four rivets; Helm: 'And a cowbell. That's the funny bone of the drum set!', a crash-splash by the cowbell, 'the Jimmy Reed cymbal'; a 1960s Ludwig Speed King pedal; 'I love that wooden rim... it actually knocks better if it's wood'; Pro Mark, Zildjian, Slingerland (about two years), Yamaha before. Interviewer on The Girl I Left Behind: 'A fat 2 & 4 back beat, and it sits so far behind it almost steps into the next bar!' (Helm: it may be Amy playing). Justin Guip on Dirt Farmer: 20x14 kick, 6x14 snare, 12x8 rack, 14x14 floor; toms taped down, a pillow in the kick with a ported front head, a Zero Ring and tape on the snare, 'Just when I thought they were dead, Levon would deaden them a little more'; Blasticks and Hot Rods on some songs; 'He likes a deader sound'; all A Zildjian: 17-inch medium crash with rivets on his left, 20-inch medium crash ride with rivets on the right, 18-inch thin crash on the right, 14-inch New Beat hats; 'a very distinctive bell tone'. The interviewer lists Ringo Starr, Jim Keltner, Richie Hayward, George Receli and Steve Jordan among the drummers who respect him.

title: Scott Jordan, 'Backtalk with Levon Helm', OffBeat, December 1998
notes: 'My first big hero was Pat Curtis, with Sonny Boy [Williamson], the King Biscuit Boy' (Peck Curtis); Curtis's home-made brush of copper-wrapped piano strings on a wooden handle, 'the first hot rod'; 'Walcott had a nine-piece band, and had a left-handed drummer with three tom-toms that was real good'; 'We were drum-poor right there in my part of Arkansas'; Bubba Stewart and Curtis the only two he knew with a kit, both lent theirs; 'listening to Earl [Palmer], and the Memphis records with D.J. Fontana'; 'Earl Palmer has got to be the greatest rock and roll drummer that's still around'; the 'Keep a Knockin'' kick-off 'one of the greatest hooks in music'; a fill he thought was his own that Palmer had already played on a Little Richard record; 'concentrated so much on that wooden-sounding backbeat, with lots of stick and skin in the sound, not much metal-that hard Memphis knock'; 'I've always been pulled into that Memphis drum sound'; 'We're all rhythm section guys... That's what The Band was'; 'I can't really sound my best until I've got the bass player and the piano player'; New Orleans records 'my cup of tea right from the very front'.

title: Levon Helm, 'The Music', Razor, February 2004
notes: In his own words. 'Between their left-handed drummer and James "Peck" Curtis, Sonny Boy Williamson's drummer, I knew exactly where I wanted to sit' (Walcott's show); Curtis left the King Biscuit kit at KFFA, where he could use it; Bubba Stewart, drummer in Ralph DeJarnette's band at a Marvell pool hall, 'never minded how many questions I had' and later lent his white oyster pearl Slingerland for a Hawks gig; 'Bubba continued to coach me on playing the drums until he could pass me over to Jack Nance and Tommy "Porkchop" Markham', two of Conway Twitty's drummers; W.S. Holland, Carl Perkins's drummer, 'plays left-handed and right-footed most of the time'; 'D.J.'s drum parts changed Elvis, Scotty and Bill's good rockin' trio into one of the top notch rock'n' roll bands in the Memphis area'; Dylan's fans 'booed at the sight of my red sparkle ... drum kit'; Richard Manuel 'one of the best natural-born drummers I ever heard'; Danko's 'joyfully loose bass playing fit my drumming like a glove'; Ringo befriended him, later hired him.

title: Ken Micallef, 'The Great Levon Helm', Modern Drummer (web preview of the April 2008 interview by Steve Jordan), 16 February 2008
notes: Preview only; the full interview is in the April 2008 issue, not read. Jordan: 'The shuffle against the straight 8th is the key to rock 'n' roll.' Helm: 'if the song is in a street-beat kind of a feel... I'll sing in more of a shuffle rhythm. Then you get the two rubbing against each other. That's what Earl [Palmer] taught us. He would do it in the same song... He would play the shuffle and the straight 8th... I kind of copied from Earl, I'm sure'; sing 'off those two beats mainly', 'play the downbeat and the backbeat with it'; 'get in that right place and then bounce on top of it'. Jordan: 'Levon plays the song'. Micallef: 'Perhaps the greatest singer/drummer to ever play a backbeat'; 'Deep South drumming'. Keltner, as quoted: drummers who have heard him 'all say how much they love and appreciate what he does'.

title: Levon Helm, 'Levon Helm on Drums and Drumming' / 'Classic Rock, Country and Blues Drumming', Homespun Tapes, 1992
notes: Read through YouTube's automatic captions, so quoted loosely: Homespun's own clips HXCt-yAv7Ns ('Hang Up My Rock and Roll Shoes', with Randy Ciarlante on a second kit) and 1E0dm6YIZEw, and gRekuHyIgXU and dyrAwfc-FPg; the full video (5GdnbkTTBPg, 103 min) has no captions and was not watched. Elderly Instruments' listing names The Weight, King Harvest, Short Fat Fanny, Up on Cripple Creek and Life Is a Carnival among the parts he teaches. Helm: 'if you center the bass drum more onto the one it'll steady the music... At the same time it doesn't hem yourself in. You can still have lots of fun and be very loose with... either hand'; with two drummers 'one of us sort of holds down the triplicate feel, leaves the other one clear to go', the other breaking it up 'into more of a jazz type feel'; 'if you can get the two of them rubbing together you can create... an illusion between the bass drum and your sock cymbal... and your snare drum'; 'if I get a chance to hit that cowbell it's always good for me'; 'if your drums don't sound good put some tape on them... choke them down, muffle them down a little bit; if a cymbal's too bright, same thing'; halving a busy feel 'gives the music more space'. Dixie: 'you march right along'.

title: 'Inside Jim Keltner's Drumming Style', Drum Channel, 14 May 2025
notes: Keltner names Hal Blaine and Charlie Watts as favourites, 'And there are others like Levon who played one hit on the tom-tom, and it would go right through your body.'

title: Marc Myers, 'The Weight by the Band's Robbie Robertson', Wall Street Journal, 29 November 2016 (as quoted by Scott K. Fish)
notes: Robertson: 'At some point during rehearsals, I stumbled across Levon adjusting his drumheads and the sounds they made. ... I had him loosen the heads so when he hit them, the sound would slide to another tonality.' The WSJ original was not read; Fish's blog quotes it.

title: The Last Waltz - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 121,136. 25 November 1976, Winterland Ballroom, San Francisco; opened with Up on Cripple Creek; Don't Do It the encore; Ringo Starr on drums for I Shall Be Released and both jams; The Weight in the film is the Staple Singers soundstage version filmed later at MGM; John Simon: the live recording was fixed in post-production, 'Only Levon's part was retained in its entirety'; cameras Michael Chapman, László Kovács, Vilmos Zsigmond and others; the La traviata set and chandeliers; triple album 16 April 1978, film 26 April 1978; Helm's criticism in his autobiography.

title: The Band (album) - Wikipedia
notes: 22 September 1969, Capitol, John Simon; Sammy Davis Jr.'s pool house, 8850 Evanview Drive, Hollywood Hills; Up on Cripple Creek, Whispering Pines and Jemima Surrender at the Hit Factory, New York; Helm lead on Rag Mama Rag, The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down, Up on Cripple Creek, Jemima Surrender; Helm credited with drums, mandolin, guitar; Manuel with drums too; Christgau A+; No. 9; National Recording Registry 2009.

title: Music from Big Pink - Wikipedia

title: Rock of Ages (The Band album) - Wikipedia
notes: 15 August 1972, Capitol; recorded 28-31 December 1971 at the Academy of Music, New York; Allen Toussaint's horn charts for five horns (Howard Johnson, Snooky Young, Joe Farrell, Earl McIntyre, J.D. Parron); Helm drums, mandolin; Manuel also credited with drums; Don't Do It, King Harvest, Dixie, Rag Mama Rag, The Weight, Life Is a Carnival, Chest Fever.

title: Northern Lights - Southern Cross - Wikipedia
notes: November 1975, Capitol, produced by the Band at Shangri-La, Zuma Beach, spring-summer 1975; Helm drums, guitar, percussion, vocals; Manuel also credited with drums; Ophelia (Helm lead), Acadian Driftwood, It Makes No Difference. Helm called it 'the best album we had done since The Band' (The Band article).

title: Dirt Farmer - Wikipedia
notes: 30 October 2007, Vanguard; produced by Larry Campbell and Amy Helm at Levon Helm Studio, Woodstock; drums Levon and Amy Helm; percussion Byron Isaacs and George Receli; Best Traditional Folk Album, 50th Grammys (February 2008).

title: Richard Manuel - Wikipedia
notes: 'In the Band era he would occasionally assume the drummer's stool when Helm played mandolin or guitar.' 'His loose, improvisatory drumming style was notably different from Helm's taut, soul-influenced approach', on Rag Mama Rag and Evangeline.

notes: The first line-up (1989): Ringo Starr (vocals, drums), Levon Helm (drums, mandolin, harmonica, vocals), Jim Keltner (drums), Rick Danko, Joe Walsh, Nils Lofgren, Dr. John, Billy Preston, Clarence Clemons; live album 1990.

title: Vintage Drum Forum, 'Levon Helm snare on Last Waltz' and related threads
notes: Posters' guesses from photos: a natural-finish wood snare with wood hoops; a Gretsch (round badge) kit in pearl for the concert and a wood-hoop pawn-shop Ludwig in the soundstage scenes (The Weight with the Staples, Evangeline with Emmylou Harris); the pawn-shop kit bought in Los Angeles before The Band (1969). Nobody cites a primary source.
